subject: math
cluster: Reason quantitatively and use units to solve problems
intro: This quiz checks whether you can define and choose appropriate quantities and units when building a descriptive model of a real-world situation. For each question, pick the single best, well-defined quantity for the stated goal.

items.prompt:
A coach wants to model how fast each runner moves during a $100$ meter sprint. Which quantity, with its unit, best captures a runner's speed?
A) Distance run, in meters
B) Speed, in meters per second
C) Race time, in seconds
D) Speed, in meters
items.answer: B) Speed, in meters per second

steps: Speed is a rate: a distance divided by a time, so its unit must combine a length unit with a time unit, namely meters per second.
Option B names the right quantity (speed) with a correct rate unit (meters per second), so it is the best choice.
Option A reports only distance in meters, which by itself does not describe how fast the runner moves.
Option C reports only the time in seconds, which again is not a speed.
Option D attaches the wrong unit: speed cannot be measured in meters, because that is a length, not a rate (inconsistent unit misconception).
solution.answer: B) Speed, in meters per second

items.prompt:
A store manager wants to model how much money the store takes in each day. Which quantity, with its unit, best fits this goal?
A) Number of customers, in people
B) Daily revenue, in dollars per day
C) Store size, in square feet
D) Daily revenue, in dollars per customer
items.answer: B) Daily revenue, in dollars per day

steps: The goal is money taken in each day, so the quantity should be a total amount of money per day, measured in dollars per day.
Option B names daily revenue with the unit dollars per day, matching the goal exactly.
Option A counts customers, which is relevant to the business but is not the money taken in (off-target quantity).
Option C measures store size, which is irrelevant to daily money taken in.
Option D uses dollars per customer, which is revenue per customer, not the daily total the question asks for (wrong scale for the goal).
solution.answer: B) Daily revenue, in dollars per day

items.prompt:
A scientist measures the average height of adult sunflowers in a field to build a model. Which choice states a reasonable unit and level of precision for this quantity?
A) Height, to the nearest foot
B) Height, to the nearest thousandth of an inch
C) Height, in pounds
D) Height, allowing values up to $500$ feet
items.answer: A) Height, to the nearest foot

steps: Adult sunflowers are typically a few feet tall, so measuring to the nearest foot is a sensible unit and a reasonable level of precision for a descriptive model.
Option A uses a length unit and a precision that fits the context, so it is the best choice.
Option B demands precision to the nearest thousandth of an inch, far more detail than the quantity warrants (unreasonable precision misconception).
Option C uses pounds, a unit of weight, not a unit of height (inconsistent unit).
Option D allows heights up to $500$ feet, an absurd range for a sunflower (unreasonable range).
solution.answer: A) Height, to the nearest foot

items.prompt:
City $P$ has $900{,}000$ residents and City $Q$ has $150{,}000$ residents. To decide which city is more crowded, which quantity should you define?
A) Total population, in people
B) Population density, in people per square mile
C) Land area, in square miles
D) Total population, in people per square mile
items.answer: B) Population density, in people per square mile

steps: Crowdedness compares how many people share a given area, so a fair comparison needs a per-unit-area quantity, not a raw total.
Option B defines population density in people per square mile, which lets you compare cities of different sizes fairly.
Option A compares total population, but a bigger city is not necessarily more crowded, so raw totals mislead here (raw total instead of per-unit misconception).
Option C reports land area alone, which says nothing about how many people occupy that area.
Option D pairs the word total population with a density unit, mixing a count with a per-area unit inconsistently.
solution.answer: B) Population density, in people per square mile

items.prompt:
School $M$ had $400$ students pass a state exam and School $N$ had $250$ students pass. The schools enroll very different numbers of students. To compare how well the two schools performed, which quantity should you define?
A) Number of students who passed, as a count
B) Percent of students who passed, as a percent
C) Total enrollment, in students
D) Number of students who passed, in percent
items.answer: B) Percent of students who passed, as a percent

steps: Because the schools enroll different numbers of students, comparing raw counts of passers is unfair, so you need a quantity scaled to enrollment.
Option B defines the percent of students who passed, which fairly compares performance across schools of different size.
Option A uses a raw count of passers, which favors the larger school regardless of performance (count instead of percent misconception).
Option C measures total enrollment, which is off target for judging performance.
Option D labels a raw count of students as a percent, confusing a count with a percent (mismatched type and unit).
solution.answer: B) Percent of students who passed, as a percent

items.prompt:
To compare two amusement parks, a student proposes the quantity 'how fun the park is.' For a descriptive model, what is the main problem with this quantity, and what is a better replacement?
A) It is fine as is, because everyone knows what fun means
B) It is not operationally well defined; replace it with average wait time per ride, in minutes
C) It is too precise; replace it with the exact number of atoms in the park
D) It is irrelevant; replace it with the park's ticket price, in dollars, to judge how fun it is
items.answer: B) It is not operationally well defined; replace it with average wait time per ride, in minutes

steps: A quantity in a model must be operationally well defined, meaning two observers could measure it and agree on the value.
'How fun the park is' cannot be measured this way, so it is not well defined; average wait time per ride, in minutes, is measurable and comparable, making Option B correct.
Option A wrongly accepts a vague, unmeasurable quantity (not-well-defined misconception).
Option C misdiagnoses the problem as too much precision and offers an unmeasurable, absurd replacement.
Option D replaces fun with ticket price, an off-target quantity that does not measure how fun the park is (irrelevant quantity).
solution.answer: B) It is not operationally well defined; replace it with average wait time per ride, in minutes

items.prompt:
You are choosing between two cell phone plans. Plan $X$ costs $\$30$ per month plus $\$0.10$ per GB of data; Plan $Y$ costs $\$45$ per month with unlimited data. You want to model total yearly cost as a function of monthly data use $d$, measured in GB. Which set of quantities, with units, is sufficient and well defined for this model?
A) Monthly data use $d$ in GB, and total yearly cost in dollars per year
B) Total yearly cost in dollars per year only
C) Number of phone calls, as a count, and total yearly cost in dollars
D) Monthly data use $d$ in GB, and total yearly cost in dollars per GB
items.answer: A) Monthly data use $d$ in GB, and total yearly cost in dollars per year

steps: To model yearly cost as a function of monthly data use, you need the input quantity (monthly data use $d$ in GB) and the output quantity (total yearly cost in dollars per year).
Option A defines both quantities with correct, consistent units, so it is sufficient and well defined for the model.
Option B names only the output, so it cannot be written as a function of data use because the input quantity is missing (insufficient set).
Option C includes number of phone calls, an off-target quantity, and omits the data-use input the plans depend on (irrelevant and insufficient).
Option D gives the cost output in dollars per GB rather than dollars per year, the wrong unit for a yearly total cost (inconsistent unit).
solution.answer: A) Monthly data use $d$ in GB, and total yearly cost in dollars per year

items.prompt:
Farm $A$ harvests $1{,}200{,}000$ kg of tomatoes from $40$ hectares, and Farm $B$ harvests $400{,}000$ kg from $8$ hectares. To decide which farm is more productive per unit of land, which quantity should you define, and what value does it take for the more productive farm?
A) Total harvest, in kg; Farm $A$ is more productive with $1{,}200{,}000$ kg
B) Yield, in kg per hectare; Farm $B$ is more productive with $50{,}000$ kg per hectare
C) Yield, in kg per hectare; Farm $A$ is more productive with $30{,}000$ kg per hectare
D) Total harvest, in kg per hectare; Farm $A$ is more productive with $1{,}200{,}000$ kg per hectare
items.answer: B) Yield, in kg per hectare; Farm $B$ is more productive with $50{,}000$ kg per hectare

steps: Productivity per unit of land is a rate, so you must define yield in kg per hectare rather than compare raw totals.
Farm $A$ yield: $\frac{1{,}200{,}000 \text{ kg}}{40 \text{ ha}} = 30{,}000$ kg per hectare.
Farm $B$ yield: $\frac{400{,}000 \text{ kg}}{8 \text{ ha}} = 50{,}000$ kg per hectare, which is larger, so Farm $B$ is more productive per hectare. Option B is correct.
Option A compares total harvest, a raw total that ignores land area and so answers the wrong question (raw total misconception).
Option C uses the right quantity but picks Farm $A$, whose yield $30{,}000$ kg per hectare is smaller than Farm $B$'s $50{,}000$ kg per hectare.
Option D labels a raw total as kg per hectare, mixing a total with a per-area unit inconsistently.
solution.answer: B) Yield, in kg per hectare; Farm $B$ is more productive with $50{,}000$ kg per hectare
